subject: Not a big deal but a bit annoying:  I wanted to use the Matt trick but I got tangled up in the definition of parameters

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Not a big deal but a bit annoying:  I wanted to use the Matt trick but I got tangled up in the definition of parameters
parts:
Hi all. I’ve attached my data, R script, and Stan programs. Here was the first version of my Stan program (saved in the file worldcup.stan, attached):

data {
int nteams;
int ngames;
vector[nteams] prior_score;
int team1[ngames];
int team2[ngames];
vector[ngames] score1;
vector[ngames] score2;
real df;
}
transformed data {
vector[ngames] dif;
vector[ngames] sqrt_dif;
dif <- score1 - score2;
for (i in 1:ngames)
sqrt_dif[i] <- (step(dif[i]) - .5)*sqrt(fabs(dif[i]));
}
parameters {
real b;
real<lower=0> sigma_a;
real<lower=0> sigma_y;
vector[nteams] a;
}
model {
a ~ normal(b*prior_score, sigma_a);
for (i in 1:ngames)
sqrt_dif[i] ~ student_t(df, a[team1[i]]-a[team2[i]], sigma_y);
}

It ran ok but I thought that to be clean I should use the Matt trick on the group-level parameters “a”:

eta ~ normal(0, 1);
a <- b*prior_score + sigma_a*eta;

This would seem to be no problem, as I could simply declare “eta” in the parameters block.
But, then, what do I do with “a”? It can’t be a parameter because it’s assigned. So I put it into the model. But I wanted to return “a”, so I had to redefine it in the generated quantities block. But to do so I had to copy code.

Ugly ugly ugly ugly hackkity hackkity hackkity hack. See attached worldcup_matt.stan.

Anyway, the Matt-trick’d program converged ok but two problems remain:

(1) The program is ugly and messy. This is bad news because I wanted to use it as an example of how easy Stan is! Maybe we can figure out a way to implement the Matt trick using functions or something like that, in some way that the programs don’t become so ugly?

(2) Both models gave me the following informational message a couple times during warmup:

Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::normal_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter is 0:0, but must be > 0!
If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

I’m confused here. The scale parameter of the student_t here is sigma_y which is constrained to be positive. So I don’t understand how it could be 0. I followed the instructions and ignored the message but it still bothers me.

My larger problem, though, is I don’t like to have to tie myself into knots in the programming in order to tell Stan how to do things right. The Matt trick for hierarchical models comes up almost every time I run Stan, so maybe there’s a way for us to implement it more cleanly?

A

Hi all. I apologize for sending the previous message. I’d forgotten about the “transformed parameters” block. This helped a lot. The model is still a bit ugly but much less so than before (see attached for convenience).

I’m still getting those informational messages, though, like this one:
Informational Message: The current Metropolis proposal is about to be rejected because of the following issue:
Error in function stan::prob::student_t_log(N4stan5agrad3varE): Scale parameter is inf:0, but must be finite!

If this warning occurs sporadically, such as for highly constrained variable types like covariance matrices, then the sampler is fine,
but if this warning occurs often then your model may be either severely ill-conditioned or misspecified.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] sorry, ignore (most of) the last message
parts:
Welcome to the club of users bothered by that message.

Yes, the constraint says lower=0, but the problem is
that we're dealing with limited-precision (64-bit
double precision, to be specific) floating point numbers,
and they don't behave like continuous quantities.

The transform we use is exp() to map the unconstrained
parameters back to positive parameters. If x < -800 or so,
exp(x) = 0. It underflows to 0 use more precise terminology.
To illustrate in R, consider:

> log(exp(-800))
[1] -Inf

Hmm. Shouldn't that be -800? No, because exp(-800) underflows to 0
and log(0) is -Inf.

Have you been following the umpteen discussions on these
messages we've had? Most recently last week?

Do you have an opinion as to what we should do about the messages?
The behavior's pretty much built into floating point unless we change
the transform we use.

The current plan (in my mind at least) is to remove any hint of
the words "error" or "warning" and point users to a longer discussion
in the manual of what's going on with floating point and ill-conditioned
posteriors.

As to making the non-centered parameterization (formerly known as
the matt trick) built in, maybe we could define a density directly for
it and save the user doing anything at all. I'll have to think about it,
and while waiting for lunch is perhaps not the best time for that...

- Bob
